# Read in the mtcars dataset:

Make sure you have set RStudio's Working Directory to your STATS 10 Lab Folder:

**Session** -\> **Set Working Directory** -\> **Choose Directory**

**IMPORTANT: Run the chunk below FIRST! We will need this data to complete the lab!**

```{r}
# Glossary:
# mpg: Miles/(US) gallon
# cyl: Number of cylinders
# disp: Displacement (cu.in.)
# hp: Gross horsepower
# drat: Rear axle ratio
# wt: Weight (1000 lbs)
# qsec: 1/4 mile time
# vs: Engine (0 = V-shaped, 1 = straight)
# am: Transmission (0 = automatic, 1 = manual)
# gear: Number of forward gears
# carb: Number of carburetors
# Source: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/datasets/versions/3.6.2/topics/mtcars

mtcars_df <- mtcars
head(mtcars_df)
```

# Code Examples (this part is to assist you with the report, do not include in your submission)

## Scatterplot
```{r}
# y ~ x means that we are plotting the variables y on the y-axis and x on the x-axis
# We use these arguments to plot the data and label the scatter plot:
# main: Title the plot (character)
# xlab: Label the horizontal or x-axis (character)
# ylab: Label the vertical or y-axis (character)
# col: The colors of the points (character); see https://r-charts.com/colors/
# pch: The symbols of the points (numerical); see https://r-charts.com/base-r/pch-symbols/
# cex: The sizes of the points (numerical)

plot(
  mtcars_df$mpg ~ mtcars_df$wt,
  main = "Miles per Gallon versus Weight",
  xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
  ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
  col = "red",
  pch = 3,
  cex = 1.5
)
```

## Correlation
```{r}
# cor(): Return the correlation coefficient between two vectors
cor(mtcars_df$mpg, mtcars_df$wt)
```

## Simple Linear Regression Models
```{r}
# lm: Fit a linear model.
# y ~ x: Specify that y and x are your DEPENDENT and INDEPENDENT variables
# data: The data frame or table from which we are pulling the values
# summary(): Print a summary table for the model
# You can read the goodness of fit (R-squared) from the summary table
linear_model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars_df)
summary(linear_model)
```

## Plotting Regression Lines
```{r}
# We use abline(model_name) to add regression lines to scatterplots
# Below, we have the same scatterplot as above.
# We use abline(linear_model) to add the regression line to it.
# lwd: Line width
# lty: Line type (lty = 2 makes dashed lines); see https://r-charts.com/base-r/line-types/

plot(
  mtcars_df$mpg ~ mtcars_df$wt,
  main = "Miles per Gallon versus Weight",
  xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
  ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
  col = "red",
  pch = 3,
  cex = 1.5
)
abline(linear_model, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
```

# Lab Exercises

Question 1. Explain the difference between the correlation coefficient and the goodness of fit value.

**Answer:** The goodness of fit is the square of the correlation coefficient and explains
how much of the variation in the dependent variable is explained by the independent variable.

Question 2. Choose two variables other than `mpg` and `wt` from the mtcars dataset (you can use only one of `mpg` or `wt`).
Create a scatterplot and calculate/print the correlation coefficient. Interpret the correlation coefficient for your chosen two variables.

**Scatterplot**
```{r}
# Fill in the dots based on the two variables you choose!
# Scroll up to the "Scatterplot" example to see how.

plot(
  mtcars_df$mpg ~ mtcars_df$hp,
  main = "Miles per Gallon versus Horsepower",
  xlab = "Gross Horsepower",
  ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
  col = "red",
  pch = 3,
  cex = 1.5
)
```

**Correlation**
```{r}
# Fill in the dots based on the two variables you choose!
# Scroll up to the "Correlation" example to see how.

cor(mtcars_df$mpg, mtcars_df$hp)
```

**Answer:** There's a strong negative correlation between MPG and gross horsepower.

Question 3. Using the same two variables from **Question 2**, create a linear regression line and plot it on the scatterplot.
What is the intercept and slope coefficients, and what do they mean in the context of the data?

**Linear Regression**
```{r}
# Fill in the dots based on the variables you choose!
# Scroll up to the "Simple Linear Regression Models" example to see how.

mtcars_model <- lm(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars_df)
summary(mtcars_model)
```

**Regression Line**
```{r}
# Exactly the same scatterplot code as in Question 2
# We only add abline(mtcars_model) at the end to add the line

plot(
  mtcars_df$mpg ~ mtcars_df$hp,
  main = "Miles per Gallon versus Horsepower",
  xlab = "Gross Horsepower",
  ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
  col = "red",
  pch = 3,
  cex = 1.5
)
abline(mtcars_model, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
```

**Answer:** The intercept is 30.09 MPG, and the slope is -0.068 MPG per gross horsepower.
Since the data doesn't contain 0 horsepower, we can't really assign any meaning to it.
We can still interpret the slope, though.
It indicates that for each increase by 1 in gross horsepower
the MPG of a car decreases on average by -0.068 MPG.

Question 4. Explain whether the linear regression line is a good model for the chosen variables from **Question 2**. 

```{r}
plot(mtcars_model, which = 1)
```

**Answer:** The residuals appear to be randomly scattered around 0 with no apparent
pattern, so combined with the high r-value we can conclude that the LR line
is a decent model for MPG vs HP.

Question 5. Using the Iris dataset from Lab 2, create a scatterplot of two variables of your choosing with
a linear regression line. Is the linear regression model a good fit? Explain your answer. (Hint:
You may want to use a Residual Plot to support your explanation.)

Let's load in the dataset first:
```{r}
url <- "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/iris/iris.data"
iris_df <- read.csv(url,
  header = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Sepal.Length",
    "Sepal.Width",
    "Petal.Length",
    "Petal.Width",
    "Species"
  )
)
```

and then create our scatterplot and linear model:
```{r}
iris_model <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris_df)
summary(iris_model)
```

```{r}
plot(
  iris$Petal.Length ~ iris$Sepal.Length,
  main = "Petal Length vs Sepal Length",
  xlab = "Sepal Length",
  ylab = "Petal Length",
  col = "red",
  pch = 3,
  cex = 1.5
)
abline(iris_model, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
```

Finally, we can use the residual plot to analyze the quality of the fit:
```{r}
plot(iris_model, which = 1)
```

Although the R-squared value is decent, there does some to be some sort of pattern
going on in the residual plot, with two generally parallel trends slanting down.
I can only say that it's a decent fit.

Question 6. Using the same variables in the Iris dataset from #5, find the correlation coefficient without
using the cor() function. Interpret the correlation coefficient in terms of the two variables.
```{r}
# Shorthands
petal <- iris_df$Petal.Length
sepal <- iris_df$Sepal.Length

z_petal <- (petal - mean(petal)) / sd(petal)
z_sepal <- (sepal - mean(sepal)) / sd(sepal)
r <- 1 / (nrow(iris_df) - 1) * sum(z_petal * z_sepal)

sprintf("Manual r-value: %f", r)
sprintf("Internal r-value: %f", cor(petal, sepal))
```
The r-value indicates a strong positive correlation between the petal length and sepal length.
